prompt: A company needs 80,000 aluminum housings per year. Each housing has thin ribs, several bosses, a general dimensional tolerance of ±0.20 mm, and two bearing bores that require ±0.015 mm after processing. Compare machining from billet with near-net-shape casting followed by finish machining of the bores. Discuss tooling cost, material yield, cycle time, repeatability, and the need for secondary machining rather than assuming one process is universally best.
intent: Select and compare manufacturing routes using geometry, tolerance, volume, and economics.

prompt: A 50 mm diameter steel shaft is turned at a cutting speed of 180 m/min with a feed of 0.25 mm/rev. The tool travels 120 mm along the part and allowance for approach is neglected. Calculate the spindle speed, axial feed rate, and approximate cutting time. Then explain one reason why simply increasing cutting speed may reduce rather than improve sustained productivity.
intent: Calculate turning parameters and relate speed to tool life and productivity.

prompt: A bent sheet-steel bracket consistently springs open by about 2.5° after unloading. Material lot records show yield strength increased by 12% while thickness and tooling are unchanged. Explain the likely mechanism, how the material change can affect springback, and two process or tooling adjustments that could be evaluated without assuming the nominal bend angle alone controls the final geometry.
intent: Relate material behavior and bending process parameters to springback.

prompt: An aluminum casting has rounded internal voids in several regions, but a separate defect cluster appears only at a thick junction that is last to solidify. Explain how the evidence can distinguish gas porosity from shrinkage porosity, why the thick junction is a hot-spot risk, and what gating/feeding or solidification changes should be investigated.
intent: Diagnose casting porosity using morphology and solidification evidence.

prompt: An injection-molded polypropylene cover previously cooled for 18 s and was dimensionally stable. Cooling was reduced to 11 s to increase output, after which warpage rose sharply while fill pressure and part mass stayed similar. Explain how cooling time, mold temperature, through-thickness temperature gradients, shrinkage, and residual stress could interact, and identify measurements that would test the explanation.
intent: Diagnose polymer warpage after a cycle-time change.

prompt: A pressed ceramic compact has a green density of 58% of theoretical density. After sintering it reaches 94% of theoretical density and its linear dimensions shrink by 14%. Explain why compaction density is not final density, why sintering is not the same as bulk melting, and how nonuniform green density can contribute to distortion or cracking.
intent: Connect powder compaction, sintering, densification, and dimensional change.

prompt: Two batches of the same quenched steel reach similar hardness immediately after quenching. Batch A is tempered at a lower temperature than Batch B. Explain the expected qualitative differences in hardness, toughness, residual stress, and dimensional stability, and why choosing the hardest condition is not automatically the best manufacturing decision.
intent: Reason about quench-and-temper trade-offs in production.

prompt: A shop is choosing between two alloys for a high-volume machined fitting. Alloy X has 15% higher tensile strength but causes roughly twice the tool wear and requires 25% lower cutting speed; Alloy Y meets the design strength requirement with margin and machines cleanly. Explain why selecting the 'strongest' alloy can increase total manufacturing cost and what additional service and process evidence should drive the choice.
intent: Evaluate practical material selection using machinability and service requirements.

prompt: A sliding guide develops polished grooves and debris, while an adjacent exposed fastener shows reddish corrosion products. Explain why these observations indicate different degradation mechanisms, what evidence would distinguish abrasive/adhesive wear from corrosion, and why a corrosion-resistant coating alone may not solve the guide problem.
intent: Distinguish wear from corrosion in a manufacturing system.

prompt: A 600 mm long aluminum fixture is calibrated at 20°C and used at 32°C. Use a linear thermal-expansion coefficient of 23×10^-6 /°C. Estimate the length increase and explain how this could bias a tight dimensional inspection if the part and fixture are at different temperatures.
intent: Quantify thermal expansion and connect it to dimensional metrology.

prompt: A steel support operates continuously at elevated temperature under a load well below its room-temperature yield strength. After long service it shows permanent elongation. Explain why this may be creep rather than ordinary elastic deformation, what variables govern creep risk, and why room-temperature strength alone is insufficient for the assessment.
intent: Distinguish creep from elastic deformation in service.

prompt: A fiber-reinforced composite panel is very stiff along the fiber direction but deflects more than expected transverse to the fibers. Explain why anisotropy matters to machining, drilling, fastening, and dimensional prediction, and why a single scalar 'strength' value is inadequate for manufacturing decisions.
intent: Apply composite anisotropy to manufacturing and assembly.

prompt: A micrometer repeatedly reads a 25.000 mm reference as 25.018, 25.019, 25.018, and 25.019 mm. Explain what this pattern says about precision/repeatability versus accuracy/bias, what calibration or adjustment actions are justified, and why high resolution on the display would not by itself make the measurement accurate.
intent: Distinguish repeatability, bias, accuracy, resolution, and calibration.

prompt: A gauge R&R study estimates standard deviations of 0.006 mm from repeatability, 0.004 mm from reproducibility, and 0.008 mm from true part-to-part variation. Treat the components as independent. Estimate the combined measurement-system standard deviation and compare it with part-to-part variation. Explain why a large measurement contribution can make an apparently variable process difficult to diagnose.
intent: Quantify measurement variation and separate it from part variation.

prompt: A hole is specified as 20.000 to 20.030 mm and a mating shaft as 19.980 to 20.010 mm. Calculate the minimum and maximum possible clearance. State whether the fit is always clearance, always interference, or can transition between the two, and explain why nominal dimensions alone are insufficient.
intent: Compute worst-case fit and interpret assembly behavior.

prompt: A flange has a bolt-hole pattern whose function is to align with a mating housing. Inspectors currently check each hole's X and Y coordinates from arbitrary part edges, but the edges are not functionally important and vary after trimming. Explain why a datum system tied to the functional mounting surfaces would improve interpretation of location error, without requiring symbol memorization.
intent: Explain functional datum selection and positional control.

prompt: An X-bar chart has all points inside its 3-sigma control limits, but the process mean is only 0.02 mm below the upper specification limit and many individual parts fail inspection. Explain why 'in control' does not mean 'capable,' distinguish control limits from specification limits, and state what additional data are needed to assess capability.
intent: Distinguish statistical stability from specification conformance.

prompt: A stable process produces a diameter with mean 15.000 mm and standard deviation 0.040 mm; specification is 15.000±0.080 mm. Without relying only on a capability label, explain why this process is centered yet still marginal/incapable by common capability expectations, and identify whether reducing spread or shifting the mean is the more relevant improvement.
intent: Reason about a centered but excessively variable process.

prompt: A batch contains 1,000 units. Inspection finds 70 total defects distributed across 50 defective units. Of the 1,000 units, 930 pass all steps the first time, 45 are successfully reworked, and 25 are scrapped. Calculate first-pass yield, final good-unit yield after rework, and explain why '70 defects' is not the same as '70 defectives.'
intent: Calculate yield measures and distinguish defects from defectives.

prompt: A job-shop has three work centers. Orders frequently wait several days before Work Center 2 even though its average utilization is only 72%. Product routes differ and arrivals are highly variable. Explain how variability, sequencing, batch release, and temporary congestion can create long queues even when average utilization is below 100%, and what data should be examined before buying another machine.
intent: Reason about queues and routing in a variable job-shop.

prompt: A factory is considering moving a product family from departmental machines into a manufacturing cell. The family has moderate volume, similar routings, and frequent handoffs between departments. Explain the likely effects on travel, WIP, visual control, flexibility, and equipment utilization, including one reason a cell could be a poor choice.
intent: Evaluate cellular manufacturing as a system design choice.

prompt: Demand is rising by 20%. Management proposes buying a second milling machine because the existing mill runs 88% of scheduled time. However, downstream heat treatment limits output to 900 parts/week while the mill can supply 1,150 parts/week. Analyze the actual capacity constraint and compare alternatives such as heat-treatment expansion, scheduling changes, outsourcing, or process improvement.
intent: Identify the true system constraint before capacity investment.

prompt: An automated press will not start. The HMI shows Start command ON, guard-closed sensor ON, hydraulic pressure permissive ON, but the part-present sensor remains OFF even though a part is physically in the nest. Explain how to separate a sensor/wiring problem from logic or process-state problems and describe a safe diagnostic sequence without bypassing the interlock.
intent: Troubleshoot a failed start permissive safely.

prompt: A dryer suddenly reports product temperature 18°C above normal, yet an independent handheld probe and product quality remain unchanged. The installed temperature transmitter also shows a gradual zero shift during weekly checks. Explain why the sensor should be treated as evidence rather than physical truth and how to confirm whether the process or measurement channel changed.
intent: Distinguish sensor drift from a real process excursion.

prompt: A robot places parts with a spread of only ±0.05 mm around its taught position, but the average placement is consistently 0.8 mm away from the required fixture location. Explain the difference between repeatability and accuracy and identify calibration, coordinate-frame, tooling, or fixture checks that are more relevant than simply slowing the robot.
intent: Distinguish robotic repeatability from absolute accuracy.

prompt: A robot cell's pick-and-place motion is sped up by 15%, but total cell throughput falls 6% and fault stops increase. Logs show the downstream vision station has unchanged inspection time, queue occupancy before vision is frequently full, and robot gripper vacuum alarms increased. Explain how a local speed increase can reduce system throughput and identify the hidden constraints and reliability trade-offs.
intent: Analyze why faster robot motion can reduce cell throughput.

prompt: A temperature-control loop oscillates after a controller gain increase. The heater saturates at 100% during each recovery, the temperature sensor has about 20 s of filtering delay, and the process itself has a long thermal lag. Explain how controller aggressiveness, sensor delay, process lag, and actuator saturation can interact, and propose a safer tuning/diagnostic strategy than further increasing gain.
intent: Diagnose control-loop oscillation with lag and saturation.

prompt: A pneumatic cylinder is commanded to extend. The PLC output indicator turns ON and the solenoid coil measures correct voltage, but the cylinder does not move; air supply pressure upstream is normal and the valve exhaust sounds abnormal. Identify the most plausible fault classes and what checks distinguish actuator/valve, mechanical jam, downstream restriction, and logic problems.
intent: Separate logic, actuator, and physical-process faults.

prompt: A machine has MTBF = 120 h and MTTR = 6 h. Using steady-state availability A = MTBF/(MTBF+MTTR), calculate inherent availability. Then explain why two machines with the same reliability can have different availability if their repair times differ.
intent: Calculate availability and distinguish it from reliability.

prompt: Vibration at 1× running speed on a motor-pump set has doubled over three months while overall flow and pressure remain normal. Axial vibration is also elevated, bearing temperature is unchanged, and the coupling was recently replaced. Discuss misalignment, imbalance, looseness, and sensor error as competing hypotheses and identify measurements that would discriminate among them.
intent: Diagnose a vibration trend without overclaiming the mechanism.

prompt: A critical machine uses a gearbox that fails on average once every four years, but replacement lead time is 14 weeks and a failure stops the line. The spare costs €18,000 and can degrade if stored poorly. Explain the spare-parts decision using downtime consequence, lead time, failure probability, preservation, and possible repair/loan alternatives.
intent: Evaluate a critical spare-parts strategy.

prompt: A furnace heats 500 kg of steel from 25°C to 825°C each batch. Use an average specific heat of 0.60 kJ/(kg·K). If furnace-to-load efficiency is 40%, estimate the required input energy in MJ, ignoring phase change. Then explain why actual energy use may be higher due to furnace walls, exhaust, openings, and soak time.
intent: Apply an industrial energy balance to process heating.

prompt: An injection mold has a 6 mm thick region that cools much more slowly than surrounding 2 mm walls and produces sink/warpage. Explain qualitatively how conduction distance, local heat capacity, coolant-channel placement, and cycle time interact. Identify process or design changes that could improve uniform cooling.
intent: Connect heat transfer to molding quality and cycle time.

prompt: A compressed-air header is at 7.0 bar(g), but a tool sees only 5.1 bar(g) during peak use. Static pressure recovers when the tool stops. Explain why this pattern points toward flow-related pressure drop or restriction rather than simply proving the compressor is defective, and identify measurements to localize the loss.
intent: Distinguish supply pressure from point-of-use pressure under flow.

prompt: A 1,000 L process bath is at 12.0% concentration by volume and must be reduced to 9.0% by adding water only, assuming additive volumes and no material removal. Calculate the final bath volume and the amount of water to add. State the mass-balance assumption used.
intent: Perform a concentration dilution calculation for an industrial bath.

prompt: A cleaning bath has the correct nominal pH, but coating adhesion is poor. Conductivity has doubled and rinse-water quality recently changed. Explain why pH alone does not establish bath condition, how dissolved salts or contamination could affect cleaning/rinsing, and what measurements or controls should be checked.
intent: Interpret industrial cleaning chemistry without overrelying on pH.

prompt: A powder-drying process is suspected of leaving excess moisture that later causes blistering. Compare a direct gravimetric moisture-loss method with a spectroscopic proxy. Explain what each can establish, the need for calibration/reference samples, and why a correlation model must be validated over the production range.
intent: Evaluate analytical methods for an industrial moisture decision.

prompt: An MES reports 100% completion for a lot, but physical count shows 12 missing units and one machine's count signal is known to double-pulse occasionally. Explain why production records are not automatically physical truth, how to reconcile genealogy/count data with floor evidence, and what data-quality controls should be added.
intent: Distinguish digital records from actual production state.

prompt: A digital twin predicts a furnace's energy use within 2% during steady production but performs poorly after maintenance changes burner tuning. Explain why model validity depends on current parameters and boundary conditions, and what revalidation or data-update steps are needed before using the twin for optimization.
intent: Evaluate digital-twin usefulness and model drift.

prompt: Plant data show defect rate is strongly correlated with outside temperature. The same hot days also coincide with higher production volume and longer machine running hours. Explain why correlation does not identify the mechanism, name plausible confounders, and specify measurements or experiments that could separate ambient-temperature effects from production-load effects.
intent: Avoid false causal inference from correlated production data.

prompt: A monthly downtime Pareto shows 42% of recorded downtime under 'minor stops,' 25% under 'material shortage,' 18% under 'maintenance,' and the rest split across other codes. Explain how to use the Pareto to prioritize investigation without assuming the largest category is already a root cause, and identify what further stratification would be useful.
intent: Use downtime data to prioritize investigation without confusing category and cause.

prompt: A hydraulic press has stopped with a worker reporting a jam near the die. System pressure is zero at the gauge, but an accumulator can store hydraulic energy and the ram is elevated. Explain the immediate hazard controls and why a zero pressure reading at one point does not prove all stored energy is dissipated. Do not propose bypassing guards or interlocks.
intent: Recognize stored-energy hazards and establish a safe state before troubleshooting.

prompt: An assembly task requires 30 N hand force, 18 reaches per minute, and repeated shoulder-level work for most of an 8-hour shift. Defects also rise near the end of the shift. Explain how force, repetition, posture, reach, and fatigue can interact, and propose workstation/process changes that reduce both ergonomic risk and error likelihood rather than blaming operators.
intent: Apply ergonomics and human-factors reasoning to production design.

prompt: A solvent-cleaning process has rising VOC emissions per finished unit even though total solvent purchase is unchanged. Production yield has fallen from 96% to 88% and rework uses additional cleaning. Explain how poor yield can worsen environmental intensity and identify prevention-oriented actions before adding end-of-pipe treatment.
intent: Connect yield loss, rework, and environmental performance.

prompt: A company can outsource a machined subassembly for 8% lower unit price, but the supplier has twice the lead time and only one qualified production site. Internal production is currently capacity-constrained. Explain the trade-offs among cost, capacity relief, resilience, quality control, flexibility, and working capital, and identify conditions under which either choice could be defensible.
intent: Evaluate outsourcing without assuming the lowest unit price is best.

prompt: A complex titanium bracket is needed in quantities of 50, 500, or 5,000 per year. Additive manufacturing avoids dedicated forming tooling and can consolidate geometry, but requires support removal, stress relief, machining of interfaces, and inspection. Conventional machining has high material waste but mature tolerance control; forging plus machining has high tooling cost but favorable material utilization at volume. Build a decision framework across volume, tolerance, finish, material properties, lead time, yield, qualification, and lifecycle cost. Do not force a single winner for all volumes.
intent: Synthesize technical and economic trade-offs among additive, machining, and forging.

prompt: A CNC-turned steel shaft gradually shifts 0.030 mm oversize over a shift while Ra surface roughness worsens from 1.2 to 2.4 µm. Machine coolant rises from 22°C to 31°C, tool flank wear increases, a reference master checked on the shop-floor gauge reads 0.008 mm high by shift end, and a cold-start geometry check the next morning is nominal. Analyze how tool wear, thermal growth, workholding, machine geometry, and measurement bias could each contribute; identify discriminating measurements; and propose a correction sequence that avoids changing multiple variables blindly.
intent: Integrate machining, thermal, metrology, and troubleshooting evidence in a dimensional-drift diagnosis.
